Doctoral student Stephen Wong (with Professor Susan Shaheen and Professor Joan Walker), from the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering at the University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley), is conducting a research project.  You are invited to participate in this study because of your experience in the recent evacuation process for the Carr Wildfire. The researchers will be obtaining your consent for this project. Why is this study being done?Disasters have a major impact on the built environment and many situations require the movement of people away from harm to reduce risk and ensure human safety.  This evacuation of people is an integral part of emergency management plans.  Despite advances in transportation management strategies, evacuations continue to cause congested conditions on transportation networks.  At the same time, vulnerable populations frequently lack adequate resources for evacuation and sheltering, and a large proportion of the population do not comply with evacuation orders.  As part of this study, we are analyzing how individuals make decisions after receiving a mandatory or recommended evacuation order.  What will happen if I take part in this research study?We will ask you survey questions related to your experience with evacuating or not evacuating your residence during the Carr Wildfire.  These questions will include demographic information about you and your household, the address of your household, the choices you made during the event, and your opinions on the use of sharing economy platforms (i.e., technology platforms that allow the sharing of goods such as transportation and housing). If the survey includes questions you do not wish to or cannot answer, you may either choose to skip those questions, or you may choose not to participate in the study. All pieces of personal information and personal information of others will be kept as confidential as possible. Only one member from each immediate household may take the survey. You may fill out the survey at a time and place of your choosing. How long will I be in the research study?The survey will take approximately 25 minutes. Are there any potential benefits if I participate?Participants will not directly benefit from the research.  However, the results of the research may contribute to an improved understanding of individualsâ€™ decision making in disaster situations.  Will I be compensated for my time?A participant will be entered into a drawing if the participant 1) is contacted about this research, and 2) provides an email address or home address. These individuals will be eligible to win 1 of 10 Amazon Gift Cards valued at $250 each. The drawing will take place when the last survey is received. For any drawing, the odds of winning depend on how many people have a ticket entered in the drawing. As we do not know how many people will participate in this study-related drawing, we cannot predict what will be the odds of winning a prize. Individuals who win will be sent the gift cards within two weeks of the drawing through email or through their physical home address. Individuals who decline this consent form or who choose to skip questions throughout the survey will also be eligible to be entered into the drawing. However, an email address or home address must still be provided in order to send the gift card if the individual wins. Are there any other parts to this research?You will have the opportunity to indicate if you are interested in being a part of a focus group. Only individuals who mark their interest in a focus group AND provide an email address, telephone number, or physical address will be eligible. When the surveys are completed, individuals will be chosen at random to participate in a focus group. If you are chosen, you will be contacted within 3 months from the end of the surveys. Are there any potential risks or discomforts that I can expect from this study?If you experienced stress or anxiety during the evacuation process, you may remember some of these feelings and you may find it uncomfortable to answer certain questions.  However, the questions are phrased to minimize any lasting negative effects. There is also a risk of a breach of confidentiality. This risk has been minimized by using encrypted password-protected data storage and by omitting exact street addresses in any publications or reports on the research.
Will information about me and my participation be kept confidential?Your information will be kept as confidential as possible.  Confidentiality will be maintained by using encrypted password-protected data storage on the web.  Only the primary researchers will have access to this data. After submitting responses, respondents can protect their privacy by clearing their browser's history, cache, cookies, and other browsing data (warning: this will log them out of online services). Confidentiality cannot be guaranteed since data will be transmitted online and data will be stored online. How long will data be retained?Data will be retained for at most three years after the last survey has been conducted. Q36.1:
The voluntary evacuation order my neighborhood received was rescinded approximately 2 hours after it was given, being cited by the Sheriff as a "mistake". We never received a mandatory evacuation order. Before we lost electricity and cable, we had the local news on and heard about the mandatory evacuation via the news. Having the "false alarm" voluntary evacuation order in the morning allowed us all day to pack and prepare before the fire burned over. It may have been a "mistake", but it was actually helpful.
We trimmed trees, sealed attic accesses, and placed sprinklers on the roof before we left. These actions allowed fire crews to save our houses. We only left when 150-foot flames crested the nearest hill and we couldn't see our hands in front of our faces. Our primary evacuation route was cut off by fire (the firenado), so we took an alternate route. One vehicle broke down during the evacuation, so we had to offload all of the belongings out of that vehicle into the secondary vehicle and pray it was far enough away that it wouldn't be burned in the fire.
Seeing the fire pressing down on our property, and hearing about how fire crews were abandoning suppression efforts throughout the entire county, we really thought all of downtown Redding would burn. We were sure we lost the houses. And if they lost our street, there wasn't any way to keep the fire from spreading further into town.
We returned Friday morning (07/27/2018) to assess the damage after seeing a Facebook live feed of our street with some houses still standing. The video cut out one house south of us, which was standing and appeared intact, and cut back in 2 houses north of us, which were burned to rubble. We didn't know if our houses were still standing, and we had to go. Back roads weren't being monitored by local law enforcement (because they were from out of town and were unfamiliar with the area), so we were able to sneak in. The fire burned down our workshop and worked its way between our two houses, scorching walls and roofs. Spot fires were still burning around the property, so we worked to put those out. Our neighbor's house was also still on fire, so we also put a hose on it. The fire crew assigned to our street was still there, so we talked to them about what happened that night. Our efforts allowed them to save the houses, as well as our neighbor's house. We gave them access behind the houses on our side of the street (no other property has a driveway around the back like ours). They also mentioned that if we had cleared out the City of Redding greenbelt directly west of our property, we could've saved the entire street. As it was, 4 houses were completely destroyed, and at least 5 others not including ours were damaged.
As a result of the Carr Fire, my husband lost his job and has been unemployed since. The lack of working days (due to the Carr Fire, another fire in eastern Shasta County, and a fire by Mount Shasta) was cited as the main reason to close the Redding office permanently and without warning, even though the physical office was untouched. My grandmother, who lives on the property with us, likely suffered a neurological event (mini-stroke) and has been unable to maintain her independence since then. I have had to manage all the insurance claim paperwork and coordinate repairs on her behalf. We're not done cleaning up due to insurance arbitration and delayed repairs, so the property still looks like a war zone seven months later.

My husband and I were the very few people that decided to stay behind. Law enforcement and Calfire was very, very unhappy with our decision to stay. We were threatened to be â€˜hauled offâ€™ by one angry sheriff while his hand rested on his holstered gun. We got different feedback on exactly where we were allowed to be (on our property only or inside our home only). 
Once the fire passed and immediate danger was clear, LO was more relaxed about our being here. We aided in putting out spot fires, fed many animals left behind, and stayed out of everyoneâ€™s way. We carefully navigated three different neighborâ€™s yards to check on spot fires and animals. We did not have power for a week. We boiled water (it was not safe to drink) on a propane burner on the front porch. We picked vegetables and gathered eggs from neighborâ€™s yards we were protecting. My husband and I lost almost 10 pounds in the week and a half we were on lockdown out here. We bathed with garden hoses that were warmed during the day. While we were mostly sure of our safety, there were a couple of close calls where our escape routes were on fire. Also, two homes burned down two days after the fire came through (one on Saturday and one on Monday). These house fires were very close to us and the firefighters had since moved on to other areas. A couple of engines were able to respond but the homes were complete losses. We also had limited cell service and had to walk around the yard to find a signal to call 911 to report these home fires. That was extremely stressful. 
As the fire burned homes around us, the propane tanks and ammunition were exploding and it sounded like a war zone. There was little to no visibility during the day because of smoke. The darkness at night actually felt safer because you could see the glowing fire. 
Don Smith, 82, perished just up the road from our home. We watched as helicopter after helicopter swooped in with water buckets trying to save him. The pilots made a valiant effort with one chopper overheating getting so close to the flames to save Don. We didnâ€™t know what happened at the time and were devastated to learn of his heroic efforts on his dozer. I would like to make special mention of him and his bravery. He didnâ€™t know at the time the fire line he was cleaning up had not been pushed all the way through. He back tracked as the fire got more intense but didnâ€™t make it back to the clearing. We spoke to an engine captain that was on site as Don almost made it to safety. The captain started to cry recounting his story. It was a very emotional and difficult time. 
Thank you for the survey and taking an interest in this. We have made a huge effort in defensible space around our home and plan on staying home when the next fire comes through (we stayed for the 2008 lightening fires as well). We were very vigilant during this last fire...setting alarms all through the night and making walkabouts to sleeping in the driveway). Our decision to stay was sound and we would do it again in a heartbeat. Not being allowed home and not knowing if our home had been burned seemed much worse to us than staying. 
Thanks again and have a wonderful day.

Q36.1:
I spent 25 years in Sonoma County and both residential units my daughter was living in burned down in the Tubbs Fire. I studied the Tubbs Fire extensively. When the Carr fire broke out, I was immediately concerned though A safe distance in Northwest Redding, River Ridge Drive,  because of how the late afternoon wind patterns move eastward. 
The night before our neighborhood was impacted, we watched the winds push the fire within seven miles of our residence before the wind patterns during the day pushed the fire north. My wife and I started packing at 7:00 that morning though none of my neighbors seemed concerned to the least. By 10:00am, I had made three truckloads to our storage unit in another part of town of valuables for safe keeping. Removed any flammable materials, aerosols, fuels, propane tanks away. We packed both cars pointed out and watched the news incredreously as our Sheriff Bosenko refused to call an evacuation that afternoon as he did not believe Redding was in eminent danger. Late that afternoon, around 6:30, I drove two miles to the west to the Land Park Subdivision to watch the fire with my binoculars. At 6:45, I could see the easterly winds start to rapidly push the fire east. The prevailing thought was that fire had not jumped the Sacramento River or Keswick reservoir in the past and we would be spared. By 6:50, the fire has passed over Iron Mountain Road and had reached the Ridge where going downhill would lead to the Sacramento River. At 6:58pm I could see fire suddenly burning sideways down middle creek canyon  towards the Buenaventura and highway 299 intersection. I was taking pictures, so I had it recorded. Oddly, the 50 or so bystanders who lived in the neighborhood seemed unconcerned about the fire which was now two miles away. At that point, I ran two my car and sped home rapidly calling my wife to round up our three cats. Upon arriving home, it was 113 degrees, I turned off our a/c, turned off the gas to the house and rounded up the rest of what we were taking knowing that we had to go soon. The power went off at 7:25. The air was still clear with little smoke, but the wind had whipped up to at least 40 mph. At 7:39, we opened our garage doors with the emergency latches and pulled out. In the forty minutes, when I left Land Park, the fire had traveled 4-5 miles and was on the next block Spinnaker to our west. It was then that we saw the massive fire tornado spinning which was something I absolutely did not expect to see. It was only maybe 200 yards to our west away. A fire helicopter was hovering over our house and that is when we saw the first police car coming down our street to evacuate. The time was 7:40 pm.  My wife was snapping pictures and video, so I had a time stamp. We raced out of our subdivision, while we watched neighbors who had been walking their dogs not long before now panicking and loading their cars with whatever they could carry. We had planned to go north on river ridge to quartz hill, but it was obvious that was not possible. We went south and turned left on Stanford to Bellagio to Fantenell to quartz hill. Quartz hill had been closed for construction, but the barricades had been moved and we drove down to the bottom in the dirt with all the other traffic that had become instantly crazy. At the bottom we were fed by law enforcement to Benton Drive and then north on market/273. It took 30 minutes to move a half mile to lake Blvd intersection. My wife was able to get through, but I was stopped by the officer in the intersection. I kept going anyway because I knew he was just as spooked as anyone else and was going to do anything. We raced to the storage unit on Oasis road where my travel trailer was stored. Had no idea it was going to get this crazy this fast. While attaching the trailer, the power went out trapping us inside the locked gate. Debris was falling around us, even though I thought that area was completely safe. Anyway, I was able to dislodge the gate and we drove from there to friends in east Redding near Bella Vista where we set up â€œcamp.â€  around 10:00. There were massive lines of traffic. The Chevron on Oregon Trail and hwy 44 had a line of cars hundreds of yards long trying to get in. 
I went back the best I could to evacuate my best friend around midnight in north Redding. I could see the flames from most of west Redding including my neighborhood. Oddly, unlike the night before, the winds had stopped even though the temperatures were higher than the previous night when the wind was still howling easterly at the same time of night. Thankfully, I was figuring this lucky turn of events would keep the fires on the west side of Hwy 273, otherwise the fires would have pushed east into much more dense subdivisions than the areas that had been impacted. 
Overall, I felt law enforcement did the best they could given the circumstances of the County Sheriff not heading an earlier evacuation when lives certainly would have been spared. 
I have family in law enforcement and was able to get back into our neighborhood the next day very quietly. Obviously, our neighborhood had been devastated, but somehow our little section was spared. I emptied out my freezer and fridge knowing that power was a long term issue and I learned in Sonoma County that the damage from rotting meat in freezers could be awful. Oddly, a fire truck from Healdsburg pulled up and helped me as I lived in Healdsburg for 25 years and knew people on the truck.  
Later, my life and others were only spared as the tornado that was bearing down on me as we left, had made a turn from moving east to moving north. Of course that turn had tragic results for others. I have spent a lot time studying the effects of the tornado and what it did is absolutely unprecedented. My grandmothers home was lost in Paradise and what occurred there is certainly awful after driving around. The tornado was a completely different animal. It devoured everything in its path. Trees, soil, rocks, just everything. Two weeks later after coming back, I was walking around what I determined to be ground zero for the tornado and could smell heavy decaying animal smell. Since the landscape had been wiped clean, I determined itâ€™s source to be subterranean with snakes, and rodents that had perished in their under ground dens. 
As far as the decision making your survey is suggesting, I think the questions are that it is inherent  that people in green lawn subdivisions donâ€™t consider themselves at risk. And fire is just as inherently unpredictable and even the experts never would have figured a fire tornado would form and move as quickly as it did. Here, I planned better than nearly all of my neighbors and yet it still was flawed.  
Bottom line is that agencyâ€™s have to prepare their communities to act and act rapidly in a precise fashion. There really is no safe outcome other than to try and minimize loss of life the best way possible. 
We are in a time of drought and growing climate extremes. Today, I saw photographs of my area from a 100 years ago and the first thought was the complete lack of foliage including trees on the hillsides nearby. Had that still been the case, Carr fire never would have happened as there would not have been anything to burn. We will just have to manage and make some choices that people wonâ€™t be happy with in regards to our forests.

Q36.1:
The biggest issue in evacuations for the Carr Fire was the lack of timely, accurate emergency communications - even PRIOR to the rapid spread of the fire and the fire-tornado on 07/26/18 in the late afternoon/early evening. The CodeRED mobile alert system did not work for those of us who had previously registered (not ONE person I know or met received any alerts until long after their neighborhoods were gone - even though law enforcement said they were sending them out). The "regular" emergency alerts only worked on some people's mobile phones (only on my teen daughter's in our household, and very few people in my neighborhood or that I met after the evacuations received them) despite the phones' settings allowing them. The initial "regular" emergency alerts received on my daughter's and one neighbor's phones were very unclear for our neighborhood, our part of town, and were inconsistent throughout the day. The reverse 911 call for my home was on my answering machine and time-stamped a half an hour or more after fire personnel manually evacuated those who did not receive notice and after homes in our neighborhood had already burned (confirmed to me by a firefighter friend who evacuated and fought the fire in our neighborhood).
    It would be very good if your survey prompted a comprehensive review of the emergency alert systems - with input from citizens, law enforcement, fire-personnel, and government officials.
       Your survey would be better if prior to asking about the evacuation route, you asked if we assisted other non-household members with their evacuation and if that assistance changed your evacuation route. In our case, we did assist others in another neighborhood (one that burned in the fire tornado 30 minutes after we got them out) and that clearly changed our route and evacuation choices and decisions. 
 Your survey would be easier if, instead of or along with the various choices for route, shelter, time, etc., you asked for a ranking of the considerations we felt were most important for our decisions. 
   You have a typo in the question re the date we returned home - the date the fire started is incorrect and looks to be a date from a previous fire in 2017.

Q36.1: I evacuated a church, where I am the priest. When I returned after dinner for night prayers, The roads were crowded, without any indication why. There was no evacuation order. I phoned a couple of neighbors who were not concerned. Houses all around them would burn within the next couple of hours. When I parked outside the church, burning embers were already falling around me, and the neighboring assisted living center was being evacuated. The power was off. I removed historical records and sacred artifacts from the main building, and pondered leaving it all behind to transport elders, but by that time the last of the residents were on the bus and departing the assisted living center. My home was not in imminent danger, although I could see flames, and I was pondering whether to stay or go when an employee called seeking shelter, after the "firenado" forced her to evacuate her original place of shelter. I evacuated the city in order that she could stay in my home, she left town the next day and I returned to serve (having secured the historical documents). I moved about the city, delivering supplies and providing pastoral support, but my home neighborhood was deserted, and the the area around the church remained under mandatory evacuation for the better part of a week.

Q36.1: On July 26th at 21:20 we lost our home to the Carr Fire. That morning around 0800 we received  an evacuation notice that was quickly taken back. At this point we realized the fire was very close and we evacuated our home as well as my parents home next door (they were out of town) We packed up very little and left as flames were visible. We drove 6 of the 7 cars out with 6 divers not all of which had valid US drivers licenses. After we reached our destination we received an evacuation notice at 20:54 via text message from shascom911. We believe had we not received the first evacuation notice that was taken back we would have taken everything much more seriously. My parents house was also damaged and in the end "looted" post fire. I hope that this survey helps drive a better process in the future and I would love to be part of a focus group to help drive change.

Our evacuation was a little unusual. At the time we were already planning a vacation to Oregon, with plans to leave the following day, when the fire jumped the river.  Our power went out and since I was pregnant at the time we were concerned about staying in heat and smoke, even though the fire was still some distance from our house. 
We met with our neighbors and decided to leave before it was too hard to get out, though an evacuation notice for Shasta Lake, would not go out for about 5 hours (3am) . We packed up our emergency bags and gathered our animals. We headed north on I-5. There were no hotels available until we went beyond Roseburg Oregon. Traffic was stopped going southbound. We decided to go as far as we could, get a hotel, and the next day continued to our ultimate destination in Northern Oregon. Had we not have a vacation already scheduled, we would have tried to stay locally with friends, since we knew all the hotels were already booked. As a result we stayed out of the area for over week. We had regular updates from our neighbors (who were able to stay despite the mandatory evacuation because they were law enforcement). Over time we were told about the mistakes made communicating with Shasta Lake residents. We erred on the side of safety and comfort, choosing to leave before the formal evacuations.

Q36.1:
There are quite a number of questions that have prepopulated tables giving three options which list the importance of various considerations to certain situations. They are incomprehensible.  I am highly educated and I had a lot of trouble figuring out what to do. The option groupings never fit into any choices I remotely considered as my options. This survey should have had us rate these items ourselves as to their importance to us. It would have eliminated a lot of meaningless questions. Because these questions are so confusing I highly doubt this survey will result in any information with any validity. 

This survey had only one question about pets. Many many people make decisions based on their pets needs including evacuation destinations, ability to help others, the need for space in the vehicle and the speed with which they could evacuate or plan to evacuate. All of our evacuation plans were based around our pet needs.

In addition your questions about evacuation destinations were very limited. Many of us had numerous destinations and I considered my final destination to be where I ended up before I could settle into my final temporary location. They consisted of 1 night shelter in a friends cottage, 20 miles away, our time share for 4 nights and 200 miles away and a motel for about 30 days which was 40 miles from our final residence all of which I consider the route of my evacuation. To say that my final destination is only 40 miles away is deceptive. 

I believe you needed a lot more beta testing before you rolled this out and you should have little faith in any results you infer from it.

We were very fortunate in that:
1.  We had good friends who took all 3 of us in, including our cat!  We all were very comfortable and lacked nothing.
2. Had we needed to pay for shelter, our insurance would have covered all cost.
3. We are retired and did not need to worry about work.

We had one communication by text in the morning, but it was unclear. However, that did cause us to prepare and so when we saw the fire approaching hours later, we were able to leave immediately (we never officially received a mandatory evacuation order).  All 3 of us believe it is very important to follow evacuation guidelines/recommendations/mandatory orders first before all other considerations.  But it is easier for us than many others because we have the resources to do so.

I chose to ask for help from my grown son, and stayed at his home for the duration of evacuation.  The fire itself did not threaten our structure, but occupants were not readmitted until the heavy smoke dissipated!

Hope this questionnaire gives productive ideas for the future!

As we were trying to get to the truck, 7 police and fire trucks came screaming into the Subdivison on loudspeakers yelling to get out. We were slightly behind them at this point in getting out. People were using both lanes of traffic to get out, all the way to Lake Blvd. People were driving erratically, driving off the road in the dirt, just insane. You could see the fire behind us and you could hear it. So loud.  I was terrified. We lost our home and everything we owned except a change of clothes. We were not allowed in to see the destruction for 9 days. 72 of the 94 homes on our Subdivison were completely destroyed. We have lived in 6 different places over the last 9 months. The cost of rebuilding has doubled in price, making the decision to rebuild unachievable for us. We finally bought a home, and will move later this week. We spend over 20,000 dollars in fees for house plans, city of redding costs, architect fees to get to this point. We will never recoup that money. I am not paid if Iâ€™m not at work, i missed a month of work. And hours and hours and hours more planning on the rebuild that cant happen. It has been a huge financial drain on my husband and me and the emotional loss is devastating. Iâ€™m not sure if my husband will ever be the same man again, I miss his laugh and smile. The emotional loss and damaged my very being. NO FREE AIRBNB, we are in a small 1600 sq foot house, that is an airbnb, and the cost per month is a staggering $4,600.00.  3 times my house payment for a home double the same and newer. Our home was stucco, with a concrete roof, sprinklers in every room! Many people reached out to help us, cooking food for us, clothes, shoes, gift cards for necessities. But we were also taken advantage of as CARR FIRE victims as well. The first house we found to rent, signed contract, paid deposit, she cancelled as we were preparing to move in, and I had to seek the Shasta County District Attorney to aid in receiving my deposit. Rent prices tripled, and hotels were difficult to find. The construction community has doubled prices on everything. We had insurance which promptly paid out, but no where near the amount needed to rebuild. We have wasted $20,000 and 7 months of time invested in the rebuilding process that will not be happening for us. We found a home to purchase, housing costs too have skyrocketed.f The home we bout was $100,000 dollars more than the home we lost, it is older and smaller. Personally, I hold the City of Redding and The State of California responsible, there were preventative measures pointed out, and refuted by both. We will NEVER evacuate again!!  Cal Fire lied to us when they forcibly made us leave,  Telling me that the fire was headed my way and I was in extreme danger. Car Fire took down our gates for no reason.  Our irrigated pasture stopped the fire in its tracks from their back burn.  The huge helicopter that took water out of our lake and took the shingles off our roof.

We will NEVER evacuate again because I do not trust Cal Fire to tell me the truth.  And we have in the past let people stay in our place when they were evacuated.  Plus our barns and pasture have been used for the evacuated animals.   At NO charge.
We have no share rides available in our area (13 miles west of Redding.) with a taxi costing 75 to use.

Q6.1_13_TEXT: I watched the fire coming for two days and when I saw that it may have reached populated areas, I drove out the back roads out off of Rock Creek Rd and saw the flames eating up the mountain in front of me. It was about 12:30 am in the early morning hours on July 26, 2018. I then turned around and quickly drove back out, slowing and honking when going by homes in an attempt to alert residents. On my way out, I came upon CalFire employees and asked him if they planned on evacuating the area. He said yes so I drove to my son's home nearby and got him and his household, including a bedridden elderly woman, packed and loaded up. I hauled as many people as I could fit in my vehicle on that trip, dropped them off, then went back to get more people. I got them out and as we were making one last once through the house to make sure we didn't leave important medications or other needs, their home phone rang with the Mandatory Evacuation notice. That EMS alert came in around 2:30 am. I dropped off then went back and offered assistance to an older couple who I saw struggling to get their travel trailer ready. They refused all help, stating that if they couldn't get their stuff out, their insurance would cover the loss. After I got my son's household established in my home, we watched the rest of that bright dark night and all through the day as the fire continued coming toward us. I vowed that if it jumped Keswick Lake/Sacramento River, we would need to evacuate again, this time two households in one. By 5pm, I could tell that it had jumped the lake/river and we would all need to evacuate again. While loading our trailers, we were getting covered with ash, some of which was alarmingly large. At around 6:30 pm, I watched in horror as the tornado started to form and then grew and grew and grew. I snapped two pictures of its formation before very hot bits of ... whatever ... began to fall on us, stinging bits of pain on our skin, melting into my hair. At that point, I panicked and spent a good 20 minutes running and throwing my belongings willy-nilly into our vehicles/trailers. After that firestorm had somewhat died down, I calmed again. Once we were packed and loaded, I sent everyone off to a (refuge) home in Shingletown. I stayed and waited to see if the fire would turn and because I did, I could not leave due to the congestion on all the roads so I stayed to wait for it to clear. While I was waiting, I received both a text message and a phone call with the Mandatory Evacuation notice. Then my aunt called from Texas (USFS on fire assignment) to let me know that a cousin and her two young grandchildren were stranded about a quarter mile away with a dead vehicle. I could not go to get them due to the traffic so I waited for them to walk to me. By the time they got there (she is older, overweight, and out of shape), the roads had somewhat cleared so we left, catching up to the tail end of the traffic jam at I-5 and Oasis Rd. I dropped her and her grandchildren off at her brother's house in Enterprise then started heading toward Shingletown to find my evacuated family. As I drove east through town, in my rear view mirror, I could see the flames as the fire burned into Redding. My city was on fire. It looked, and felt, like my hometown was all going to burn like everything else in that fire. It was the most surreal experience of my life.

Q36.1:
We never received any kind of notification to leave - no reverse 911, no police or city officials telling us to go. My husband had spent the day packing our cars in case we needed to leave. We were keeping our eye on the smoke. At around 6:30 pm, we could see smoke increasing but we thought we just needed to keep an eye on it. At 7:30 pm, the smoke exploded to the west. The fire was creating its own wind. I went back in the house to check on dinner when the power went off. I turned off the stove and went back outside. The smoke covered the sky to the west; we could see the cloud turning; it sounded like the biggest blow torch with things blowing up in it. I saw my neighbor loading his pick up. I asked â€œIs it time to go?â€ He said yes. (His wife was second command at the city managing this situation. He told us she would call if we needed to go. It blew up so fast she never called him.) I wanted to leave immediately but my husband didnâ€™t want us to separate. I was freaking out! We had decided that we would meet at the forest service office out by the airport. It is on the East side of I-5. His office is there. Once he got the last few things in the car, we headed out. Only to be stopped at the end of our culdesac by bumper to bumper cars. People were calm and they were letting one car from our street enter the line after one car moved forward. A police officer was at the entrance to the neighborhood. He was letting cars from our neighborhood onto Quartz Hill Road then letting cars from further down Quartz Hill Road to go. It was bumper to bumper the whole way down the hill. At one point a car from behind me sped by and almost hit a police car head on. I was able to get behind my neighbor in line. He was the engineer in charge of the construction on Quartz Hill Road. He had told us that they had worked all day on the road so that cars could drive down the road bed if needed. When we reached the road blockade city workers were there throwing the barricades down. The road was passable: we were driving on the rock. They had not started paving it yet. My husband and I were communicating through our car Bluetooth with our phones. I was really nervous as my phone was almost dead. My phone charging cord was in my trunk. When I got to Market Street, I turned into downtown Redding. Pete turned left when he got there. Pete was about 40 minutes behind me in getting to the forest service. I remember when I hit the Market St bridge I looked back and I thought there is not going to be anything left. When Pete finally got to the forest service, we took our dog and went up to his office. The last thing I took out of the house were two thermoses of soup and two bottles of water. By the time we got to the office, we were already getting texts from friends in Happy Valley who were offering their home to us. I refused to go there. Happy Valley burns every summer. After what we had been in, I wanted to get as far as possible away from any chance of the fire reaching us. Once we ate, called family and friends, we decided to try and find a place to stay. Pete started calling hotels in Anderson, Red Bluff and Chico. Everything was full. I told him to call Chico because it was off the I-5 corridor and people might not think of going there. We found a hotel there. Then started the drive. I was in the lead and truly was disoriented. I missed the turn off in Red Bluff and had to drive to Corning. We hit road work where the roads went down to one lane. It was a very difficult trip. When we got to the hotel, they would not rent us a room for longer than one night. Another evacuee helped my husband carry things out of the car to our 2nd floor room. We got there around 1 or 2 am. The next morning when my husband went to see if we could extend our stay they wanted $139 a night up $50 from the previous night. He went to the Motel 6 nearby and got us a room. It was filthy. We were just so grateful to have a place to stay. I ended up washing the floor with a bath towel. We were safe; we were together. We were okay. We knew our house had made it the next day. Our next door neighbor called. She gave us the phone number of a neighbor who had stayed through the evacuation. He went in and locked up our house. My husband left the doors unlocked in case the firemen needed to get in. Many houses in our neighborhood burned. Only 2 houses on our culdesac were damaged. We stayed in Chico 5 days. Everyone there were so nice. 2 restaurants let us take our dog onto the outside patio while we ate dinner there. We were able to move to Anderson on day 5. The hotel is  very near my school where I teach and just a few miles from the forest service. It was another Motel 6 but it was absolutely spotless. We were able to go to work each day. I took our dog with me to our classroom (school hadnâ€™t started yet). On Friday night 8 days later we heard that they might open our neighborhood from a neighbor. When we heard, we decided to leave our things in the room and went in one car. We didnâ€™t know what we would find. We had to go through two check points to get to our neighborhood. One manned by national guards and one manned by police. Everyone was concerned if our house had made it. It was incredible to see the devastation along Keswick Dam Road. Only one entrance was opened into our meighborhood. The police wanted to make sure we had s house. When we drove into the neighborhood, the first thing we saw was a house that was partially burned, next to totally burned house, next to one that was still standing next to another burned house. Most of the view houses were gone. When we turned down our culdesac, only one house was damaged. There was our house. Our dog was so happy to be home. We had no smoke damage, no damage of any kind. After checking the house, we drove back to Anderson, checked out of the hotel, and went home. It was so surreal being back before clean up started. When driving out of our culdesac, when you looked to the right it looked totally normal. When you look to the left you saw burned houses. The lots are cleaned up. Some new houses are going up, but not in many. Where the view houses were I can see what there view was. It is starting to green up in the burn. Houses are up for sale in the neighborhood and are selling. Two other memories I want to share are: first, from the night we returned to the neighborhood, in front of the only house standing in that first row of house we saw, I noticed domestic rabbits jumping around in the front yard. A few days later I saw the home owners in their front yard I stopped and asked if they were able to capture the bunnies. The woman told me that the policemen who manned the entrance to our neighborhood had set a trap that first night and caught 6 of their 8 rabbits that had gotten out. The kindness of everyone helping was heartwarming. The second memory is the smell the first time it rained. I thought it would smell clean but it didnâ€™t. It smelled even more like burnt wood. 
If we had to do it again, I would have left much earlier. We had always thought where we lived was very safe and not in danger of wildfire. We really thought we would have gotten some kind of evacuation orders. We now know how bad it could have been after the Camp Fire. We feel very fortunate and grateful for all the people who helped fight the fire and help in the recovery.

Mary Belkin

No one understood what this fire was going to do. I do believe County and City officials should have been preparing us to leave a full day sooner. Too much decision-making is being left up to citizens who have no knowledge of fire and road capacities. We rely on experts for this information. With that being said, common sense is King. We have to be responsible for ourselves when it comes to leaving. 

The morning of the evacuation I knew at some point we were going to have to leave, I began gathering items and stacking them in our living room to go into the cars at some point. We were in the middle of packing our car when law enforcement screamed from the road that we had to leave immediately. The fire had suddenly reached the hilltop. It was chaotic and terrifying. Globs of burning asphalt falling down around us, ash, smoke, tree limbs being thrown from the fire tornado, etc. Terror.

I'll say again that no one knew what this fire was going to do, but our City officials are nowhere near prepared for Wildfire or any other catastrophic event. Had the winds not shifted, had that tornado not shifted, tens of thousands of people would have died on Lake Boulevard in their cars tying to escape.

Q36.1:
I was woken up at 3 in the morning by a fireman screaming "Get out, Get out Get out!" The whole sky was red and there were explosions in the neighborhood. I was by myself (in the dark with no electricity) with cats to evacuate and no help loading my van. I phoned my husband at work first. I thought I had no time to consider packing anything personal. I grabbed 2 cats, my medications, 2 baskets of dirty laundry, my current tax info, cell phones, laptops, tablets and whatever I needed to stay in business. I went to an agreed meet-up point in Redding, stopping only to leave 2 cats at the vet. My husband, who was at work in Sacramento, drove back up I-5 (in his pickup) and back into the evacuation zone and got more cats and some personal items, like photos, jewelry, and stuff out of the safe. At that point, the fire was coming down the hill at him. We met up in Redding.

We, and 6 cats, spent the night in Redding at a friends house. The next day we caravaned to Sacramento to our parents' house. We stayed there for free in a small bedroom, with the cats, for 1.5 months and then bought a used RV. We are now living in the RV in a friends driveway in Redding, with the 6 cats, for 7 months.

It was weeks after the fire before we were allowed back into Shasta to check the property. We got the Re-population Notice via a subscribed Carr Fire e-mail sent out by the Shasta County Sheriff Office. When we got there, our house was nothing but a pile of rubble--including all the outbuildings.

And that said:

(1) Evacuation Requirement for the Carr Fire was very well communicated by officials, and online, and the Evacuation Route was open and clear. If anything, the fireman that gave me notice was overly persuasive.

(2) If I had ACTUALLY BELIEVED that my house was going to burn to the ground I would not have evacuated until my husband got home, and spent the extra 2 hours+ time packing up more things--like clothes and my kitchen appliances. I had plenty of room in my van.

I thought that the planes would be flying and that our proximity to the State Park would ensure that fire retardant would be dropped on us... as it was in past Shasta fires. I felt confident that my house and property was relatively safe. We had done all of the right things to create a defensible space. As it happened, there was nothing done by fire officials to try to save our house. In their defense, weather conditions were prohibitive. They and the news crews stood and watched it burn.

That's my story.

Q36.1:
As an evacuee the most important information you're looking for is not easily found.  The local new channel ran 24/7, but was mostly repeated information.  Only when a friend who is a retired firefighter called to see how I was doing did I find out that the best places to find information were on the CalFire, Redding FD and Shasta County Sheriff's Twitter feeds.    It was also critical to know that CalFire only updates their website fire information twice per day.

On Saturday I checked to see if the fire had spread overnight.  It looked like it had not and I felt great relief that we had finally turned the corner.  An hour later when the website was updated and I found how much it had grown I was devastated.  If I had know that the website was only updated twice per day then it would have helped to manage the emotions we were going through.

While I did not receive an official evacuation notice, when I saw on the news that the evacuation center two blocks from my home (at Shasta HS) was being evacuated - I knew it was time to leave.

Q36.1: While this survey was appropriately focused on people in their houses, 2 friends that lost their homes were away when it happened and lost everything because they were not allowed to get to their homes, including to rescue pets. Pets, I feel, are a HUGE factor in evacuating. My friend's car was Full of her pets and had no room left for mementos. I met her and took her pets (classroom pets actually) and housed/fed/cared for them for about a month. I still have the guinea pigs since they still don't have a home and the school was only Just reopened. But if you call places that serve pets, There was a whole "Cowboy 911" set up. Like, the reptile store and turtle rescue were getting escorts in to rescue reptiles, and the aquarium store was getting escorts to rescue salt water tanks and Cal Fire was letting the house burn to save the barn full of animals. It seemed like every open corner had an RV with animal cages who couldn't go to the Red Cross shelter. Our local Pet Smart had employees sheltering in their break room... with their pets. Animals and children hold our heart strings and are whom most of us are making the decisions for.... not for ourselves but how do we save them? The final count for me was 57 friends evacuated, 8 lost everything. Of the 8 that lost everything, 2 lost their pets. I was pretty sure I was safe the whole time. I offered my tiny place to any and all that I knew or people who had someone to vouch for them... but everyone knows how small my place is, so I ended up with their animals instead.
